Let $E\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable set. Let $U=L^2(E;\mathbb R)$ with inner product
$$
(q,r)_U=\int_E q(x)r(x)\,dx
$$
and the corresponding norm. This is a real Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] under Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]].

For bounds $q_a,q_b\in U$ with $q_a\le q_b$ almost everywhere, define the **admissible box**
$$
Q_{ad}(q_a,q_b)=\{q\in U:q_a(x)\le q(x)\le q_b(x)\text{ for almost every }x\in E\}.
$$
Equalities and inequalities between controls are understood as almost-everywhere statements about their $L^2$ classes. The box is nonempty because it contains $q_a$. When a finite-element control space is used, its cellwise-constant admissible set is the intersection of this box with the stated piecewise-constant subspace; cellwise averaging preserves the box when both bounds are constant on each control cell.

derivations.claim: The control $q_a$ belongs to $Q_{ad}$ because $q_a\le q_a\le q_b$ almost everywhere, so $Q_{ad}$ is nonempty. If $q,r\in Q_{ad}$ and $0\le t\le1$, then $q_a\le tq+(1-t)r\le q_b$ almost everywhere; hence the convex combination is in $Q_{ad}$. The pointwise inequality also gives $|q|\le |q_a|+|q_b|$ almost everywhere for each $q\in Q_{ad}$, so $\|q\|_{L^2}\le\|q_a\|_{L^2}+\|q_b\|_{L^2}$ and the box is bounded.

Suppose $q_n\in Q_{ad}$ and $q_n\to q$ in $L^2(E)$. For almost every $x$, $q_n(x)\ge q_a(x)$, so $(q_a-q)^+\le |q_n-q|$ almost everywhere, where $s^+=\max\{s,0\}$. Therefore $\|(q_a-q)^+\|_2\le\|q_n-q\|_2\to0$ and $q\ge q_a$ almost everywhere. Similarly $(q-q_b)^+\le|q-q_n|$ gives $q\le q_b$ almost everywhere. Thus $q\in Q_{ad}$ and the box is norm closed.

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

For each $k \in \mathbb{N}$ let $I_k = [a_k, b_k]$ be a closed bounded interval
with $a_k \le b_k$ ([[def-interval]]), and suppose the family is **nested**:

$$I_{k+1} \subseteq I_k \qquad (k \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $\ell_k = b_k - a_k \ge 0$ for the length of $I_k$. Then:

1. $\displaystyle\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k$ is **nonempty**. More precisely,
   with $a = \sup\{a_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$ and
   $b = \inf\{b_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$, both of which exist, one has $a \le b$
   and $$\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k = [a, b].$$
2. $\displaystyle\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k$ is a **single point** if and only
   if $\ell_k \to 0$ ([[def-real-limit]]).

Every hypothesis is load bearing. Dropping closedness makes the intersection
empty; dropping boundedness does the same; and dropping nonemptiness of the
individual intervals is vacuously fatal.

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

Recall that a natural number is a von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$ and $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, so
that

$$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$$

is itself the set of its predecessors. Here $<$ is the order of
[[def-nat-order]], which is defined additively, so the displayed identity is a
theorem and not a convention: it is [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]], proved
immediately above. Let $A$ be a set, and let $\approx$ be equinumerosity
([[def-equinumerous]]).

- $A$ is **finite** if $A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **countably infinite** if $A \approx \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite.
- $A$ is **uncountable** if it is not at most countable.

If $D$ is finite, a finite listing from its bijection with a natural number, repeated periodically, gives a sequence; if $D$ is countably infinite, a bijection with $\mathbb N$ gives a sequence. Thus [F4] supplies a dense sequence $(v_j)_{j\ge1}$ without any choice principle beyond the witnesses in the definition of countability.

For any bounded real sequence $(a_k)$ in $[-R,R]$, start with $I_0=[-R,R]$. At each stage split the current interval into its two closed halves and choose the left half if it contains infinitely many terms of the current sequence, and otherwise choose the right half. At least one half contains infinitely many terms. Choose the least index later than the preceding selected index whose term lies in the chosen half. The resulting nested intervals have lengths tending to zero, so [F1] gives a common point, and the selected subsequence converges to it. Every choice in this construction is the least natural index or the leftmost of two alternatives, so the extraction is determined by its input sequence.

For each $j$, the scalar sequence $\langle x_n,v_j\rangle_H$ is bounded by $C\|v_j\|_H$ by [F3]. Apply the deterministic extraction in step 1.2 successively to these coordinate sequences, each time inside the previously obtained subsequence. This recursive rule produces nested infinite subsequences $N_1\supseteq N_2\supseteq\cdots$ on which the first, first two, and then first $j$ pairings converge, respectively. Let $n_k$ be the $k$th index of $N_k$. Nestedness makes $(n_k)$ strictly increasing, and for each fixed $j$ the sequence $\langle x_{n_k},v_j\rangle_H$ converges because its tail is a subsequence of $N_j$.

For any $v\in H$, choose $v_j$ arbitrarily close to $v$. For indices $k,\ell$, [F3] gives $|\langle x_{n_k}-x_{n_\ell},v\rangle_H| \le |\langle x_{n_k}-x_{n_\ell},v_j\rangle_H|+2C\|v-v_j\|_H.$ The first term tends to zero as $k,\ell\to\infty$ for fixed $j$, and the second can be made arbitrarily small by density. Thus $\langle x_{n_k},v\rangle_H$ converges for every $v$. Its limit $L(v)$ is linear and satisfies $|L(v)|\le C\|v\|_H$, so $L$ is a bounded linear functional. By [F2] there is a unique $x\in H$ with $L(v)=\langle x,v\rangle_H$ for all $v$. Therefore $x_{n_k}\rightharpoonup x$.

If $A$ had positive measure, then for some integer $m\ge1$ the measurable set $A_m=\{x:q(x)\le q_a(x)-1/m\}$ would have positive measure, because $A=\bigcup_{m\ge1}A_m$. Weak convergence and $q_n\ge q_a$ give $\int_{A_m}(q-q_a)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{A_m}(q_n-q_a)\ge0,$ whereas the definition of $A_m$ makes the left side at most $-\mu(A_m)/m<0$. Apply the same argument to $B=\{x:q(x)>q_b(x)\}$ and $B_m=\{x:q(x)\ge q_b(x)+1/m\}$. Weak convergence gives $\int_{B_m}(q-q_b)=\lim_n\int_{B_m}(q_n-q_b)\le0$, while the defining inequality on $B_m$ makes this integral at least $\mu(B_m)/m>0$ if $B_m$ has positive measure. Thus $q\le q_b$ almost everywhere, and [F1] gives $q\in Q_{ad}$.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, $V=H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and $H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. Use the real integral pairing on $H$. Equip $V$ with the standard full Sobolev inner product and norm
$$(v,w)_V=(v,w)_H+\sum_{i=1}^d(D_i v,D_i w)_H,\qquad \|v\|_V^2=\|v\|_H^2+\sum_{i=1}^d\|D_i v\|_H^2.$$
Here $H^1_0=W^{1,2}_0$ is the closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ in the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]. Under Countable Choice, $H$ and $V$ are real Hilbert spaces; the local proof of completeness of $V$ is included in [[thm-linear-elliptic-control-state-and-adjoint-wellposedness]]. The inclusion $J:V\to H$ is continuous with $\|J\|\le1$.

Let $E\subseteq\Omega$ be bounded and measurable, $U=L^2(E;\mathbb R)$ with its real integral inner product, and let $Q_{ad}\subset U$ be the pointwise box of [[def-pde-box-control-set]]. Under Countable Choice, $U$ is a real Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Let $a:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be bilinear, bounded with constant $M$, and coercive with constant $\beta>0$ in the stated $V$ norm; symmetry is not assumed. Let $B:U\to V^*$ be bounded and linear, and fix $f\in V^*$, $u_d\in H$, and $\alpha>0$.

For every $q\in U$, the **state** $u(q)\in V$ is required to satisfy
$$
a(u(q),v)=\langle f+Bq,v\rangle_{V^*,V}\qquad(v\in V).
$$
The reduced objective, defined on all of $U$ and minimized over $Q_{ad}$, is
$$
\widehat J(q)=\frac12\|Ju(q)-u_d\|_H^2+\frac\alpha2\|q\|_U^2.
$$

$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$,
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, and $u,v,w\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$. If both
$v$ and $w$ are weak $\alpha$-derivatives of $u$, then
$$v=w\quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Omega.$$
Thus a weak derivative, when it exists, is unique as an almost-everywhere
class. No connectedness assumption is needed.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the assertion holds because there is only the zero
class and no nonzero tests.

Let $(v_n)$ be Cauchy in this norm. Its function coordinates and each of its finitely many weak-derivative coordinates are Cauchy in $L^2(\Omega)$ because each coordinate norm is bounded by the full $W^{1,2}$ norm. By [F3], there are $v,g_1,\ldots,g_d\in L^2(\Omega)$ with $v_n\to v$ and $D_i v_n\to g_i$ in $L^2$ for each $i$.

For every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ and $i$, the weak-derivative identity for $v_n$ is $\int_\Omega v_nD_i\varphi=-\int_\Omega (D_i v_n)\varphi$. By [F5], both test functions are in $L^2$; Cauchy–Schwarz lets both integrals pass to the limits in [F3], giving $\int_\Omega vD_i\varphi=-\int_\Omega g_i\varphi$. Thus each $g_i$ is a weak derivative of $v$. By uniqueness in [F4], $D_i v=g_i$ as an $L^2$ class, and the component convergences from step 1.1 give $v_n\to v$ in the full $W^{1,2}$ norm. Subtracting the two state equations gives $a(w_h,v)=\langle Bh,v\rangle$ for all $v$, so $w_h$ depends linearly and boundedly on $h$ by the state estimate in [F1]. Expanding the two squared norms in $\widehat J(q+h)$ yields $\widehat J(q+h)-\widehat J(q) =(Ju(q)-u_d,Jw_h)_H+\alpha(q,h)_U+\frac12\|Sh\|_H^2+\frac\alpha2\|h\|_U^2.$ The adjoint equation with $v=w_h$ and the state variation equation with test $p(q)$ give $(Ju(q)-u_d,Jw_h)_H=a(w_h,p(q))=\langle Bh,p(q)\rangle=(B^*p(q),h)_U$. derivations.claim: The box is nonempty by [F1], so $m:=\inf_{q\in Q_{ad}}\widehat J(q)$ is finite: $\widehat J\ge0$ and $\widehat J(q_a)<\infty$. By Countable Choice choose $q_n\in Q_{ad}$ with $\widehat J(q_n)<m+1/n$. Since $\widehat J(q_n)\ge\alpha\|q_n\|_U^2/2$, the sequence is bounded. By [F2], a subsequence converges weakly to some $q\in U$, and [F1] gives $q\in Q_{ad}$.

If $q_*$ minimizes, fix $v\in Q_{ad}$. Convexity gives $q_*+t(v-q_*)\in Q_{ad}$ for $0\le t\le1$. Minimality makes the right directional quotient nonnegative for every $t>0$; letting $t\downarrow0$ and using [F4] proves the variational inequality.

Write $Ju(q_n)-u_d=J u(0)-u_d+S q_n$. Bounded linear maps preserve weak convergence, so along the subsequence this state residual converges weakly in $H$ to $Ju(q)-u_d$; the controls converge weakly in $U$. The Hilbert norm is weakly lower semicontinuous: if $z\ne0$, then $\|z_n\|\ge |(z_n,z/\|z\|)|\to\|z\|$, while the case $z=0$ is immediate. Applying this to both squared norms in $\widehat J$ gives $\widehat J(q)\le\liminf_n\widehat J(q_n)=m$. Thus $q$ attains the infimum.

The exact expansion in [F3] shows strict convexity: for distinct $q,r\in U$ and $0<t<1$, $\widehat J(tq+(1-t)r)=t\widehat J(q)+(1-t)\widehat J(r)-\frac{t(1-t)}2\bigl(\|S(q-r)\|_H^2+\alpha\|q-r\|_U^2\bigr).$ The last subtracted term is positive, so two different minimizers in the convex box cannot exist.

Conversely, if $q$ satisfies the variational inequality, then for every $v\in Q_{ad}$ the exact expansion [F3] gives $\widehat J(v)-\widehat J(q)=(B^*p(q)+\alpha q,v-q)_U+\frac12\|S(v-q)\|_H^2+\frac\alpha2\|v-q\|_U^2\ge0.$ Thus $q$ is a minimizer; step 3.1 gives uniqueness.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ be an affine bijection from a bounded open
set $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ to $K$, where $A$ is invertible, and let
$1\le p\le\infty$. For every integer $r\ge0$ and scalar
$v\in W^{r,p}(K)$, the pullback $\widehat v:=v\circ F$ belongs to
$W^{r,p}(\widehat K)$. For $r\ge1$ its first weak derivatives satisfy
$$D_{\widehat x_j}\widehat v=\sum_{i=1}^d A_{ij}(D_{x_i}v)\circ F,$$
and higher derivatives are obtained by applying this constant-matrix rule
repeatedly. In particular, for each $0\le m\le r$,
$$|\widehat v|_{W^{m,p}(\widehat K)}\le C(d,m)\|A\|^m|\det A|^{-1/p}|v|_{W^{m,p}(K)},$$
where $|\det A|^{-1/p}:=1$ for $p=\infty$. The reverse estimate holds
with $A^{-1}$ and $|\det A|^{1/p}$ in place of $A$ and
$|\det A|^{-1/p}$.

Assume Countable Choice. For every $1\le p<\infty$ there is
$C_{d,p}<\infty$ such that for all
$u\in W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d;\mathbb R)$,
$$\|u-u_{\widehat S_d}\|_{L^p(\widehat S_d)} \le C_{d,p}|u|_{W^{1,p}(\widehat S_d)},\qquad u_{\widehat S_d}:=|\widehat S_d|^{-1}\int_{\widehat S_d}u\,dx.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

$$(v,w)_V=(v,w)_H+\sum_{i=1}^d(D_i v,D_i w)_H,\qquad \|v\|_V^2=\|v\|_H^2+\sum_{i=1}^d\|D_i v\|_H^2.$$
Here $H^1_0=W^{1,2}_0$ is the closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ in the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]. Under Countable Choice, $H$ and $V$ are real Hilbert spaces; the local proof of completeness of $V$ is included in [[thm-linear-elliptic-control-state-and-adjoint-wellposedness]]. The inclusion $J:V\to H$ is continuous with $\|J\|\le1$.

Let $E\subseteq\Omega$ be bounded and measurable, $U=L^2(E;\mathbb R)$ with its real integral inner product, and let $Q_{ad}\subset U$ be the pointwise box of [[def-pde-box-control-set]]. Under Countable Choice, $U$ is a real Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Let $a:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be bilinear, bounded with constant $M$, and coercive with constant $\beta>0$ in the stated $V$ norm; symmetry is not assumed. Let $B:U\to V^*$ be bounded and linear, and fix $f\in V^*$, $u_d\in H$, and $\alpha>0$.

For every $q\in U$, the **state** $u(q)\in V$ is required to satisfy
$$
a(u(q),v)=\langle f+Bq,v\rangle_{V^*,V}\qquad(v\in V).
$$
The reduced objective, defined on all of $U$ and minimized over $Q_{ad}$, is
$$
\widehat J(q)=\frac12\|Ju(q)-u_d\|_H^2+\frac\alpha2\|q\|_U^2.
$$
A spatially varying coefficient, boundary control, variational crimes, finite-element control discretization, and parabolic evolution are separate hypotheses or branches; none is implicit in this definition. The state well-definedness is supplied by [[thm-linear-elliptic-control-state-and-adjoint-wellposedness]].

Assume Countable Choice and the setting of [[def-linear-elliptic-pde-constrained-control-problem]]. For every $q\in U$, there is a unique state $u(q)\in V$ satisfying
$$
a(u(q),v)=\langle f+Bq,v\rangle\qquad(v\in V),
$$
and
$$
\|u(q)\|_V\le \beta^{-1}\|f+Bq\|_{V^*}.
$$
For every $q\in U$, there is also a unique adjoint $p(q)\in V$ satisfying
$$
a(v,p(q))=(Ju(q)-u_d,Jv)_H\qquad(v\in V),
$$
with
$$
\|p(q)\|_V\le \beta^{-1}\|J\|\,\|Ju(q)-u_d\|_H.
$$

Let $V_h\subseteq V$ be finite-dimensional, and let $a_h:V_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ and $F_h:V_h\to\mathbb K$ be bounded, with $F_h$ having the same test-linearity as $F$, and $a_h$ coercive with constant $\alpha_h>0$ in the inherited norm. $$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\left((1+M/\alpha_h)\|u-v_h\|_V+\frac{\delta_{a,h}(v_h)+\delta_{F,h}}{\alpha_h}\right),$$

where the defects are those of [[def-variational-crime-error-framework]]. For a family of meshes this is a uniform estimate whenever $\inf_h\alpha_h>0$ and the displayed approximation and defect terms are uniformly controlled. The term $\delta_{F,h}$ retains source approximation and data oscillation.

$$

$$

$$
(B^*p,h)_U=\langle Bh,p\rangle_{V^*,V}.
$$

$$
\alpha\|h\|_U^2\le ((S^*S+\alpha I)h,h)_U\le(\|S\|^2+\alpha)\|h\|_U^2.
$$
Consequently $\nabla\widehat J$ is Lipschitz with constant $L=\|S\|^2+\alpha$, and $\widehat J$ is $\alpha$-strongly convex.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T>0$, let $V$ be a separable real Hilbert
space, and let $(V,H,V^*)$ be its real evolution triple. Suppose
$a(t;\cdot,\cdot):V\times V\to\mathbb R$ is bilinear and scalar measurable
for each fixed pair $v,w\in V$, and there is one null set outside which
$$|a(t;v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad a(t;v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2$$
for all $v,w\in V$, with constants $M>0$ and $\alpha>0$. Let
$f\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$ and $u_0\in H$. Then there is a unique
$u\in W(0,T;V)$ with $u(0)=u_0$ and, for almost every $t$,
$$\langle u'(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}+a(t;u(t),v) =\langle f(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\qquad(v\in V).$$
For every $t\in[0,T]$ it satisfies
$$\|u(t)\|_H^2+\alpha\int_0^t\|u(s)\|_V^2\,ds \le\|u_0\|_H^2+\alpha^{-1}\int_0^t\|f(s)\|_{V^*}^2\,ds.$$
The proof applies BNB to the space-time form. Scalar measurability suffices
because $V$ is separable and the measurable inverse action is proved locally.

Let $V$ and $H$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective,
continuous linear map with dense range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real linear
dual of $V$. Identify $H$ with its Hilbert dual by its inner product and embed
$H$ into $V^*$ by
$$h\longmapsto\bigl(v\longmapsto (h,i v)_H\bigr).$$
The resulting dense continuous embeddings are written
$$V\hookrightarrow H\cong H^*\hookrightarrow V^*$$
and $(V,H,V^*)$ is called an **evolution triple**. The pairing between $V^*$
and $V$ is denoted $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$.

For a Hilbert space $X$, $L^2(0,T;X)$ is the space of equivalence classes of
strongly measurable $X$-valued functions $w$ with
$$\int_0^T\|w(t)\|_X^2\,dt<\infty.$$
Strong measurability means being an almost-everywhere pointwise limit of
measurable simple functions. For $u\in L^2(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$,
say that $g$ is the **weak time derivative** of $u$ when
$$\int_0^T (i u(t),i v)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. The derivative is
unique up to equality almost everywhere. The **parabolic energy space** is
$$W(0,T;V):=\{u\in L^2(0,T;V):u'\in L^2(0,T;V^*)\},$$
with norm
$$\|u\|_{W(0,T;V)}:=\bigl(\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2+ \|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}^2\bigr)^{1/2}.$$
No endpoint values are part of this definition; they are assigned only after
a continuous $H$ trace representative has been proved. Separability is an
additional hypothesis when it is needed by a later result.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(V,H,V^*)$ be the real evolution triple of
[[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]], and let
$u,v\in W(0,T;V)$. Each has a unique representative in $C([0,T];H)$, and
for all $0\le s\le t\le T$,
$$\|u(t)\|_H^2-\|u(s)\|_H^2 =2\int_s^t\langle u'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\,dr,$$
$$(u(t),v(t))_H-(u(s),v(s))_H =\int_s^t\bigl(\langle u'(r),v(r)\rangle_{V^*,V} +\langle v'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\bigr)\,dr.$$
Writing $c_i=\|i:V\to H\|$, the trace obeys
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u(t)\|_H^2 \le \frac{c_i^2}{T}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2 +2\|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}.$$

$$

and the corresponding norm. This is a real Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] under Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]].

For bounds $q_a,q_b\in U$ with $q_a\le q_b$ almost everywhere, define the **admissible box**
$$
Q_{ad}(q_a,q_b)=\{q\in U:q_a(x)\le q(x)\le q_b(x)\text{ for almost every }x\in E\}.
$$
Equalities and inequalities between controls are understood as almost-everywhere statements about their $L^2$ classes. The box is nonempty because it contains $q_a$. let $u\in H^1(0,T;X)$ (meaning
$u,u'\in L^2(0,T;X)$ with distribution derivative). It has a unique
continuous representative on $[0,T]$. Let
$P\in\mathcal L(X,Y)$ be a fixed bounded linear map. Then
$Pu\in H^1(0,T;Y)$ and $(Pu)'=Pu'$.

If instead $P:[0,T]\to\mathcal L(X,Y)$ is continuously differentiable in
operator norm, then $P(t)u(t)\in H^1(0,T;Y)$ and
$$\frac{d}{dt}(P(t)u(t))=P'(t)u(t)+P(t)u'(t)\quad\text{a.e.}$$
In particular, a differentiable time-dependent Ritz comparison contributes

Assume Countable Choice and the bounded polyhedral mesh setting, spaces,
form and data of [[thm-parabolic-fem-semidiscrete-existence-energy]]. Let $u$
be the continuous solution supplied by
[[thm-parabolic-variational-wellposedness-and-energy-stability]] on the same
evolution triple and let $u_h$ be the corresponding semidiscrete solution.
For this error identity, assume the additional regularity $u\in H^1(0,T;V)$,

supplied by [[lem-parabolic-projection-time-product-rule]]. Let
$P_h:V\to V_h$ be a fixed bounded linear
comparison map, define
$$\rho(t)=P_hu(t)-u(t),\qquad\theta(t)=u_h(t)-P_hu(t),$$
and let $\mathcal R_h(t)\in V_h^*$ be the full residual
$$\mathcal R_h(t)(v_h)=(\rho'(t),v_h)_H+a(t;\rho(t),v_h).$$
Then for almost every $t$ and every $v_h\in V_h$,
$$(\theta'(t),v_h)_H+a(t;\theta(t),v_h)=-\mathcal R_h(t)(v_h),$$
and for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|\theta(t)\|_H^2+\alpha\int_0^t\|\theta(s)\|_V^2ds \le\|\theta(0)\|_H^2+ \alpha^{-1}\int_0^t\|\mathcal R_h(s)\|_{V_h^*}^2ds.$$

time-dependent comparison map $P_h(t):V\to V_h$, with its time derivative
included in $\rho'$ as stated below. For a time-independent form and the
Ritz projection $P_h=R_h$ from
[[def-parabolic-ritz-projection]], Galerkin orthogonality makes
$a(\rho(t),v_h)=0$, so the residual is exactly
$(R_hu'(t)-u'(t),v_h)_H$. If a time-dependent comparison $P_h(t)$ is used,

By [A1, F1] and linearity, $z=S r$ for a bounded linear solution map $S:U\to L^2(0,T;H)$. Expanding the two squared norms gives $\widehat J(q+r)-\widehat J(q)=(u-u_d,z)_{L^2(0,T;H)}+\alpha(q,r)_U+\tfrac12\|z\|_{L^2(0,T;H)}^2+\tfrac\alpha2\|r\|_U^2.$ The last two terms are quadratic in $r$, so the first two terms give the Fr\'echet derivative once the observation residual is paired with $z$.

The transposed reversed form is measurable, bounded, and coercive with the same constants, so [A1, F1] supplies its unique energy solution; reflecting back proves [F3] and gives $p\in W$. Its weak equation is $\langle-p',v\rangle+a(t;v,p)=(g,v)_H$.
